---
title: The ROC curve, every cut at once
version: 1
---

Every metric so far needed a cut. Sometimes the question is about the model itself, before anybody
has decided where to cut: **does it put the leavers above the stayers?** The answer is a curve drawn
across every possible cut.

For each cut, compute two rates:

- the **true positive rate**, which is recall: the share of leavers who get a credit;
- the **false positive rate**: the share of stayers who get a credit, false positives over all stayers.

A cut of 1 sends nobody a credit and sits at (0, 0). A cut of 0 sends everybody one and sits at (1, 1).
Every cut in between is a point, and joining them is the **ROC curve**, from *receiver operating
characteristic*, a name it kept from its origin in radar:


Three readings of the picture:

- **The diagonal is a model that knows nothing.** Sending credits at random gives the same share of
  leavers and stayers, at every cut.
- **The further the curve bows towards the top left, the better the model separates.** The top left
  corner is every leaver found and no stayer bothered.
- **The two marked points are the two cuts of this lesson.** At 0.5 the model reaches 7.9% of leavers
  and 0.3% of stayers; at 0.278, 23.5% of leavers and 1.6% of stayers. Both sit low on the curve, which
  is where a business with a rare class and a costly action usually works.

What the curve does not show is the money. Its axes are rates, and a rate of stayers of 1.6% sounds
small until it is multiplied by 22,773 stayers and becomes 363 wasted credits, more than the leavers
reached. **On a rare class, the ROC curve makes false positives look cheap**, which is the reason for
section 08.
